title: NPPF 2026 changed the planning baseline. Your site appraisal should know that.
description: How the 17 August 2026 National Planning Policy Framework changes the way developers should structure postcode-first planning research, local-policy checks and precedent analysis.

sections.heading: The national baseline changed on 17 August 2026
body: England now has a new National Planning Policy Framework published on 17 August 2026. That matters operationally because planning histories, older officer reports and appeal decisions may have been written under a different national policy context. A development platform should therefore store the date and status of the policy material it relies on, rather than treating planning policy as static background knowledge.

For a live site, the correct sequence is to retrieve the current NPPF, the current adopted development plan, any material emerging plan, relevant neighbourhood-plan material and the local authority's current validation and supplementary guidance. National and local policy should be kept separate so the user can see which layer supports each proposition.

sections.heading: A postcode should resolve the authority before the model starts talking
body: The most basic planning-research error is using the wrong local policy because the user does not know which authority controls the site. A postcode-first workflow should geocode the site, identify the Local Planning Authority, then retrieve the authority's live planning documents. Planning Data now publishes a Local Planning Authority dataset and a Local Plan dataset that can help with discovery, although coverage and status still need verification against the authority itself.

Once the authority is known, research can move from generic search to primary documents: adopted local plan, policies map, supplementary planning documents, design codes, validation list, CIL material, parking and highways standards, biodiversity and other locally relevant guidance.

sections.heading: Precedent has to be re-read through the current policy context
body: A permission from 2023 or an appeal from 2024 can still be useful, but its weight comes from the reasoning and comparability, not the date alone. The analysis should identify which policy issues were decisive, whether those policies remain current, whether the site context is genuinely comparable and whether the technical evidence was materially different.

This is why a measured local approval sample should never be turned into a simple probability. Historic outcomes describe what happened to a retrieved group of cases. They do not replace a current assessment of the actual proposal.

sections.heading: The practical developer response
body: Build policy freshness into the feasibility workflow. Every material planning statement should retain its source, document status and retrieval date. If a local policy or obligation has not been established, leave it visible as NOT ESTABLISHED rather than allowing the appraisal or planning strategy to quietly assume it away.
The result is slower than a fake instant answer and dramatically faster than discovering after design work that the wrong planning baseline was used.

sources.name: GOV.UK — National Planning Policy Framework, 17 August 2026

title: What can you really learn from a postcode before you spend professional fees?
description: A postcode is not a due-diligence report, but it is enough to automatically assemble a surprisingly powerful first development evidence file.

sections.heading: Start with geography, not a chatbot
body: A postcode can resolve coordinates, administrative geography and the likely Local Planning Authority. From there a system can begin assembling mapping, planning and market layers before the user has written a detailed brief. That is a much stronger starting point than asking a general-purpose model what it thinks of a site it cannot actually locate.

The output should still distinguish postcode-level evidence from address- or parcel-specific evidence. A postcode centroid is useful for orientation, not proof of a boundary or precise site condition.

sections.heading: The first evidence bundle
body: A useful postcode-first bundle can include Ordnance Survey context, Google satellite and Street View, Environment Agency terrain data, planning history, Local Planning Authority discovery, current local and national policy, Land Registry sold-price evidence, current asking-market evidence, flood and environmental signals, Land Registry registration screening and nearby planning or appeal decisions.

Commercial providers can enrich that picture with floor areas, title/freehold information, property attributes, planning applications, build-cost data and current market sourcing. Each source should remain labelled so the user knows whether it is public, authoritative, licensed commercial data or AI synthesis.

sections.heading: What a postcode cannot establish
body: It cannot prove the legal boundary, measured levels, condition of structure, lawful use, drainage capacity, rights of access, contamination status, ecology, structural capacity or the acceptability of a specific design. Those are exactly the gaps the first evidence pass should expose.
The value is therefore not that the postcode answers everything. The value is that it tells the developer which questions deserve money next.

sections.heading: From site signal to site dossier
body: A sensible commercial funnel has a lightweight free screen and a substantially deeper paid intelligence process. The free screen can ask whether the user can identify the site, the current use, the biggest planning uncertainty, the obvious constraint and the next check. The paid platform then performs the live research and calculations behind those questions.
Giving away the actual live policy, title, planning-history, sold-price and appraisal work in a lead magnet destroys the distinction between marketing and product.

sources.name: HM Land Registry Price Paid Data

title: Planning prospects: useful evidence without the fake 82% approval score
description: Why the strongest planning intelligence compares policy, decisions, appeals and evidence differences instead of manufacturing a permission probability.

sections.heading: The user wants a number because the decision is expensive
body: It is understandable to want a simple approval percentage. Acquisition, design and professional fees are being committed before the authority has made a decision. The problem is that a neat percentage can imply a statistical model that does not exist. Planning decisions depend on site-specific evidence, policy, design, consultation and judgement.
A platform should resist turning sparse historic decisions into false certainty simply because percentages look commercial.

sections.heading: Use comparable decisions as evidence, not destiny
body: Nearby permissions, refusals and appeal decisions can be extremely valuable when the analysis explains why each case is comparable or distinguishable. Relevant dimensions include use, scale, massing, heritage context, access, parking, neighbour relationships, technical evidence and the policy regime at the time of decision.

The most useful output is a table of issues: what succeeded, what failed, which policy was decisive, what evidence the successful case contained and what changed between refusal and later approval where that history exists.

sections.heading: What the planning prospects engine should produce
body: Produce a lower-risk direction, a balanced direction and a higher-upside direction. For each, identify the strongest supporting evidence, the strongest vulnerabilities, the likely refusal themes and the exact surveys, drawings or professional evidence needed to test them.
If a historic positive share is shown, label it precisely as the positive share of the retrieved comparable sample. It is descriptive evidence, not a prediction of the authority's future decision.

sections.heading: The real competitive edge
body: The developer who understands the local refusal patterns and appeal reasoning before fixing the scheme can brief the design team differently. Planning intelligence is most valuable before the application becomes expensive to change.

sources.name: Planning Inspectorate appeals guidance and decisions

title: Residual land value should expose unpriced planning obligations, not quietly set them to zero
description: How to connect live planning-policy research with build cost, GDV and residual land value without pretending every local obligation can be automatically priced.

sections.heading: A residual is a subtraction problem with an evidence problem hidden inside it
body: At its simplest, residual land value is the evidence-backed gross development value less the full cost of producing the scheme and the required developer return. The arithmetic is easy. The hard part is deciding which costs and values are credible enough to enter the calculation.

A site can look attractive because the model contains detailed build and finance assumptions while the CIL, Section 106, affordable housing, abnormal works, utility upgrades or technical mitigation are simply absent.

sections.heading: Planning policy can trigger a cost without establishing its amount
body: Live policy research may establish that a CIL charging schedule applies, that affordable-housing policy is relevant or that a biodiversity, transport or drainage requirement is likely to require work. That does not automatically establish the final cash amount. The calculator should therefore create an explicit policy-cost gap rather than inserting a made-up allowance.
The correct commercial state can be: obligation potentially applicable; amount NOT ESTABLISHED; next action obtain the calculation, viability advice or professional scope required to quantify it.

sections.heading: Keep market evidence separated
body: Current asking prices describe what vendors want. Completed transactions describe achieved prices. A development model should show those evidence classes separately and explain how the GDV was formed. Where sold £/sq ft evidence is used, floor area, property type, tenure, specification and date still matter.
The user should be able to challenge every major input rather than trust a black-box valuation.

sections.heading: Stress the model before negotiating the land
body: A useful sensitivity matrix moves both GDV and build cost. The point is not to find the exact future. It is to discover how much adverse movement the deal can survive before the residual or margin becomes unacceptable.
If a small change collapses the residual, the developer has learned something material before exchange rather than after construction starts.

sources.name: HM Land Registry Price Paid Data

title: A white gap on a Land Registry map does not mean you found unregistered land
description: How developers should use HMLR INSPIRE, title information, OS mapping and Search of the Index Map without turning indicative spatial data into a legal conclusion.

sections.heading: Maps are seductive because they look definitive
body: A polygon on a map feels more certain than a paragraph of caveats. In land due diligence that can be dangerous. Ordnance Survey mapping, a title plan, HM Land Registry INSPIRE polygons, planning red-line boundaries and a measured site survey all serve different purposes.
A development platform should let the user compare those layers while preserving the distinction between them.

sections.heading: What INSPIRE can do
body: HM Land Registry's INSPIRE index polygons can be used as an indicative spatial screen of registered freehold titles. They are useful for finding title references and understanding the registered-freehold pattern around a site.

They are not the legal boundary itself and the dataset is not a complete map of every possible registered interest. A missing polygon should therefore create an investigation task, not a declaration that the land is unregistered.

sections.heading: How to confirm registration status
body: Where the question is whether land is registered, use HM Land Registry's Search of the Index Map process. Then obtain and review the relevant title/register information. If access, covenants, easements, ransom strips or ownership interpretation could affect the development, the legal review belongs inside the feasibility process rather than at the end of it.
The correct software behaviour is evidence escalation: map signal → title evidence → SIM where required → legal interpretation where material.

sections.heading: Why this matters commercially
body: Title uncertainty can alter access, developable area, planning strategy, lender appetite and value. It should therefore be visible in the development appraisal as a material uncertainty until resolved.

sources.name: HM Land Registry — Search of the Index Map

title: The local validation list is one of the least glamorous ways to save weeks on a planning application
description: Why postcode-driven planning software should retrieve the authority's current validation requirements before generating an application pack.

sections.heading: A good planning argument can still arrive invalid
body: Planning strategy and validation are different questions. An application can contain a persuasive narrative and still be delayed because a required local document, drawing, certificate or technical item is missing. That is avoidable process risk.
The local validation list should therefore be part of the first policy pack, not something checked the night before submission.

sections.heading: Validation requirements are location and proposal specific
body: A small extension, a residential conversion, a major scheme and development in a heritage or flood-sensitive location can trigger very different information requirements. The platform needs the postcode/address, proposal and current authority documents before it can build a useful checklist.
Where a requirement depends on a threshold or site characteristic that has not been established, the system should mark the trigger for verification rather than asserting the report is required.

sections.heading: Turn the checklist into commissioning briefs
body: Once likely information requirements are identified, the system can draft the question for each professional: what decision needs supporting, what evidence is already available, what the authority expects and what deliverable is required. That is far more useful than an undifferentiated consultant shopping list.
The professional still determines methodology and signs the professional output.

sections.heading: Application packs should be generated from evidence
body: A planning statement, Design and Access Statement content, validation matrix and consultant schedule should all be generated from the same source dossier. That reduces contradiction and makes it easier to update the pack when a design changes.

title: Construction does not have an AI awareness problem. It has an implementation problem.
description: Why repeatable, governed workflows matter more than giving every project manager access to another AI chatbot.

sections.heading: Access is not integration
body: Opening an AI chatbot is not the same thing as changing how project information moves through a business. The useful step is to identify recurring information friction — re-keying, searching, comparing, reporting and reconstructing decisions — and redesign the workflow around evidence, human review and clear ownership.

Government AI-adoption research published in 2026 found that large parts of UK business still neither use nor plan to use AI, with construction among the sectors showing particularly low adoption intention. Separate business-data research also found limited integration into existing systems among construction businesses already using AI.

sections.heading: Start with the loss, not the tool
body: If quotations cannot be compared, fix procurement information. If the owner spends Sunday searching email, fix retrieval. If every project lives in somebody's head, fix project memory. The first workflow should be narrow enough that the business can see whether it actually improved anything.
Define input, output, source of truth, human verification and success measure before choosing the model.

sections.heading: Governance enables scale
body: Project documents can contain personal data, prices, legal correspondence and commercially sensitive information. A serious workflow needs approved providers, access rules, retention, source provenance and a definition of what may enter the formal project record.
Governance is not the opposite of speed. It is what allows useful automation to keep working after the novelty wears off.

sections.heading: The best AI feature may be project memory
body: Decision logs, controlled variation records, document registers and evidence-linked weekly reporting are not glamorous. They are valuable precisely because they reduce the information loss that causes commercial disputes and management rework.

sources.name: UK Government — UK Business Data Survey 2026

title: Discussion is not approval: the construction variation rule that software should enforce
description: Why a controlled variation tracker should refuse to label a change approved when the evidence of approval is missing.

sections.heading: Informal communication creates false certainty
body: Construction projects move through calls, messages, site conversations and email chains. A change can be discussed by several people and still never receive clear authority on scope, price or programme. Months later, the team remembers the conversation differently.
The project record should therefore distinguish proposed, instructed, priced, approved, rejected and completed states.

sections.heading: Approval needs evidence
body: A strong system does not merely display a warning. It enforces the rule at the backend: if a user or API client tries to mark a variation Approved, the record must contain explicit approval evidence such as the approving party/date or the referenced instruction.
If that evidence does not exist, the correct state is APPROVAL NOT EVIDENCED.

sections.heading: AI can reconstruct the candidate record
body: AI can read meeting notes, emails and messages and propose a variation record: description, reason, drawing reference, quoted value, programme impact and parties involved. But it should not convert discussion into authority. The proposed record remains subject to human review.

sections.heading: This is where auditability becomes commercial
body: When the variation later affects a payment, extension of time or final account, the project has a contemporaneous evidence chain rather than a reconstructed memory. That is a much more meaningful AI benefit than generating another summary.

title: The cheapest construction quote is often the quote you understand least
description: How AI can normalise construction quotations while preserving exclusions, provisional sums and bidder wording.

sections.heading: Headline totals are not comparable scopes
body: Two quotations can appear to cover the same work while differing on access, protection, waste, temporary works, testing, making good, preliminaries, provisional sums and client-supplied items. Comparing the bottom-line figures first encourages the wrong conversation.
A normalised table should map each bidder's wording into common work packages while retaining a trace back to the original quote.

sections.heading: Ambiguity should become a question
body: The AI system should never decide that a vague sentence means an item is included. If the bidder has not established the position, the comparison should create a clarification question. This preserves the commercial value of the original evidence.

sections.heading: Comparison is not appointment
body: Scope normalisation can expose commercial differences. It is not a quantity surveyor's valuation, legal interpretation of a contract or recommendation to appoint a contractor. The user and relevant professional remain responsible for the procurement decision.

sections.heading: Store the clarification trail
body: The final clarified scope, assumptions and appointment decision should be retained in project memory. That reduces the chance that a later variation is caused by something the tender process had already discussed but failed to document.

title: A serious property deal scanner should use licensed feeds, not a fragile Rightmove scraper
description: Why compliant market-data architecture is a competitive advantage when sourcing development opportunities at scale.

sections.heading: The problem is coverage, not scraping
body: Developers want to identify reduced, unmodernised, slow-moving, unusually configured and otherwise interesting stock before manually browsing hundreds of listings. It is tempting to solve that with a crawler. For a commercial platform, that can create unnecessary legal, contractual and operational risk.
If a portal's terms restrict scraping or automated access, the stronger architecture is an authorised feed or licensed market-data provider.

sections.heading: Connect sourcing directly to feasibility
body: The sourcing feed becomes genuinely valuable when it is not a separate list of properties. Each candidate can be pushed directly into postcode/site intelligence: planning history, local policy, sold evidence, title questions, environmental constraints, likely development directions and residual-value modelling.
That closes the gap between finding a cheap-looking property and understanding why it may or may not be a development opportunity.

sections.heading: Do not call something undervalued from one ratio
body: An asking price below a local median is only a signal. Condition, floor area, tenure, title, property type, micro-location, planning position and abnormal costs can explain the difference. The system should rank investigation priority, not issue an automatic buy recommendation.

sections.heading: Data rights belong in the product design
body: A world-class platform should display provider/source provenance and respect caching, attribution and usage restrictions. Data architecture is part of product quality, not a back-office detail.
